title: Comparing and ordering numbers
keyIdea: Compare two two-digit numbers by place value: look at the tens digit first, then the ones if the tens match. Write the result with >, = or <, and order a set from smallest to largest the same way.
familyTip: Show two two-digit numbers (a door number and a bus number work well). Ask: which has more tens? If the tens match, which has more ones? Then write the comparison with > or <.

visual.caption: Which symbol fits? Drag each pair into >, = or <, or tap the pair then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: tens-first compare, ones when tens match, choose > = <, order three numbers, catch digit-sum myths.

kid: A two-digit number has tens and ones. The left digit counts tens. The right digit counts ones.
To compare two numbers, look at the tens first. More tens means a greater number.
If the tens are the same, compare the ones. 58 is greater than 52 because 8 ones beat 2 ones.
Write >, = or <. The open side of > faces the greater number. Equal means the same tens and the same ones.
adult: Ages 6 to 7. CCSS 1.NBT.3: compare two two-digit numbers based on meanings of the tens and ones digits, recording the results of comparisons with the symbols >, =, and <. National Curriculum Year 2 number and place value: compare and order numbers from 0 up to 100; use <, > and = signs.

The tens-first rule is place value, not digit size as a glyph and not the sum of the digits. 34 < 43 even though both digit-sums are 7, because 3 tens is less than 4 tens. When tens match, the ones digit decides: 58 > 52.

Common mistakes: adding the digits and calling the sums equal (3+4 = 4+3 so 34 and 43 'match'); reading a number backwards (34 as 43); choosing the number with the taller-looking digit; putting the open side of > toward the smaller number; and treating 40 as equal to 4.
In the lab your child compares with tens rods and ones cubes, picks > = < for a pair, drags three numbers into smallest-to-largest order, and catches the digit-sum myth.

practice.hint: Look at the tens digit of each number first.
practice.explain: 43 has 4 tens. 34 has only 3 tens. More tens wins, so 43 > 34.

practice.hint: Compare the tens: 4 tens versus 7 tens.
practice.explain: 4 tens is less than 7 tens, so 47 < 74. The open side of < faces the greater number.

practice.prompt: What number is {a} tens and {b} ones?
practice.hint: Tens are worth 10 each. Multiply the tens digit by 10, then add the ones.

practice.prompt: 58 and 52 have the same tens. Which is greater?
practice.hint: Same tens means compare the ones digits next.
practice.explain: Both have 5 tens. 8 ones beat 2 ones, so 58 > 52.

practice.hint: The tens digit is the left digit of a two-digit number.
practice.explain: {=10*a+b} is {a} tens and {b} ones. The tens digit is {a}.

pool.hint: Same tens and same ones means equal.
pool.explain: Both numbers are 5 tens and 5 ones, so 55 = 55.

pool.hint: 10 more means the tens digit goes up by 1. Ones stay the same.

choices: The digits add to the same sum
pool.hint: Place value: tens decide before ones or digit sums.
pool.explain: 34 has 3 tens; 43 has 4 tens. Digit sums matching does not make the numbers equal.

pool.hint: Compare the tens digits: 7 tens versus 6 tens. Ones do not override tens.
pool.explain: 70 has 7 tens; 69 has 6 tens. So 70 > 69 even though 69 has more ones.

pool.prompt: What is the ones digit of {=10*a+b}?
pool.hint: The ones digit is the right digit.
The smallest has the fewest tens.
pool.explain: 2 tens is fewer than 5 or 7, so 29 is smallest.

pool.prompt: A mix-up says 34 > 43 because 3+4 = 4+3. What went wrong?
choices: Digit sums do not decide size
pool.hint: Place value, not digit sum, decides which number is greater.
pool.explain: Adding digits is not how we compare. Tens first: 3 < 4, so 34 < 43.
